hints: Compare the two curves right after day 0. G starts high and falls, H starts at zero and rises slowly to a peak around day 12. What does that tell you about who made their own antibodies and who was just given them?
Remember that only making your own antibodies creates memory cells. Think about how a first-time primary response in a naive person compares in speed and size to a secondary memory response.
walkthrough:
**Spot passive versus active immunity**

Person G was injected with antibodies, so this is passive immunity. No antigen, no activation, no memory cells made. That is why the curve starts high on day 0 and then just falls as the antibodies break down.

Person H was injected with vaccine, so this is active immunity. The antigen activates B cells, so antibody level starts at zero, rises slowly, peaks around day 12, then falls but memory cells remain.

**Check the situation on day 20**

By day 20, G has almost zero antibody left and has no memory cells. G is essentially naive again.

H still has some circulating antibody (about 15 units) and, more importantly, has memory B cells from the vaccine.

**Predict the response to real infection on day 20**

If G meets tetanus bacteria now, G must make a primary response from scratch. That is slow, with a lag of about 10 to 14 days before antibody peaks. 20 + 12 is about day 32, so the peak will be after day 32.

If H meets the bacteria now, H will make a fast, large secondary response due to memory cells, with a peak that is higher and earlier than the first peak.

options.A: G can still produce antibodies, G just has no memory. Infection on day 20 will trigger a slow primary response.
options.B: G is naive on day 20, so a primary response takes about 10 to 14 days to peak. That puts the peak after day 32.
options.C: H has memory cells, so infection will trigger a rapid secondary rise in antibody, not a flat constant line.
options.D: The secondary response in H will be faster and higher than the first peak, not lower, because of memory B cells.
